newsitem.title: USA: Dole plans round-the-clock campaign finale.
newsitem.headline: Dole plans round-the-clock campaign finale.

text.p: Republican presidential challenger Bob Dole said on Thursday he planned to campaign around-the-clock for the last four days before election day, comparing the all-out bid to his Second World War service.
In a dramatic move to try to overcome President Bill Clinton's wide lead in the polls, he announced a 96-hour final campaign blitz to start at 12 noon EST (1700 GMT) on Friday.

"The last time I fought round the clock for my country was in 1945 in Italy," Dole said in reference to his military service, when he was gravely wounded. He made the announcement in remarks prepared for a campaign speech in Miami.
"I am determined to make every hour of this decisive election count," Dole said. "The stakes are that high."
Dole campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield said the trip would be by bus, plane and other transport and would end in the state with the most electoral votes, California.

All opinion polls show Clinton leading Dole by a comfortable margin. The Reuters tracking poll on Thursday put Clinton ahead by 7.7 points and a new poll in California showed Clinton leading by 18 points.

With time running out on a campaign that has left him struggling to catch Clinton, Dole enlisted the help of former President George Bush who appeared with him at a campaign rally in Tampa on Thursday.
"I believe in keeping the White House above partisan politics and away from these puny disputes we're seeing," Bush, who was beaten by Clinton in 1992, told the rally.

In accusing Clinton of running a partisan White House, Bush implicitly referred to brewing controversies over donations to the Democratic Party from people with ties to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.

"Bob Dole is the person to lead this country into the next millennium. What it's about is leadership. ... We need somebody to restore the respect to America around the world," Bush said in introducing his rival for the 1988 Republican presidential nomination.
At the Tampa Theatre rally, Dole told the crowd he was gaining on the Democratic incumbent. "Five big days left and the polls are going to close on Nov. 5," Dole said.
"As you know today is Halloween. All the kids are dressing up and doing scary things," Dole said. "You know, that's the way it is every day at the Clinton White House."

The former senator continued hammering Clinton on what he said was a "disastrous" economy and a "mediscare' campaign he said was frightening senior citizens who make up a large portion of the Florida population.

He said it was "irresponsible" to suggest a Dole White House would cut the popular Medicare health programme for older people. "I was the senator who helped save and strengthen Social Security. And I will be the president who saves and strengthens medicare."

He said he would name a bipartisan commission to preserve Medicare and announced he would name Democratic New York Sen. Pat Moynihan and Republican Florida Sen. Connie Mack as the first two appointments to the panel.
Dole, Bush and Mrs. Dole appeared on the same stage at the theatre. While Dole and Bush have appeared together before, this was the first time at a campaign rally.

The Doles are underscoring the importance of this state, which Bush carried four years ago. Dole then campaigns in another Southern state, Georgia, which went for Clinton four years ago, before going to Ohio, another critical state.
Florida, which has voted Republican in recent presidential elections, is the fourth largest state and has 25 of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the election.

The independent Florida Voter Poll, published by the Miami Herald on Tuesday, showed 47 percent of the state's voters favoured Clinton compared to 39 percent for Dole, eight percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and 6 percent undecided.

At a rally in a New Orleans suburb on Wednesday, Dole reminded his audience that Democrat Harry Truman came from way behind to defeat Republican Tom Dewey in 1948, a victory remembered by the photo of Truman holding up a copy of the Chicago Tribune with a large headline "Dewey defeats Truman".
"Keep your eye on me -- I'm going to be a second Harry Truman," he shouted to wild applause.
